dataset.name: Nutrient and carbon concentrations in dated soil cores at US-OWC Ameriflux wetland site (OWC NERR)
description: Soil cores were sampled at the Old Woman Creek (OWC) National Estuarine Research Reserve at the south shore of Lake Erie, near Huron, Ohio, USA. OWC is a temperate mineral soil marsh. We dated the soil cores using lead isotope analysis and measured the concentrations of carbon and nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus) throughout the core depths. We analyzed 36 cores, sampled along three transects at areas of the wetland with different hydrological regimes. Each transect included three coring sites at different water depth categories (shallow, intermediate deep) with four core samples per coring site. The data can be used to determine the carbon sequestration rates and nutrient accumulation rates, at multiple locations throughout OWC wetland.

Dataset, in csv format, with data variables in columns, and different cores and core depths slices in rows, includes results from 36 sediment cores (0-30 cm depth) taken at 9 locations (4 replicates at each location) along 3 gradients of water depth (shallow, intermediate, deep), each at a different hydrologic location (outflow, backflow, middle). At each depth slice within a core, we provide depth, date (using 210Pb), bulk density, and the concentrations of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, d13C, and d15N.

measurementTechnique:
2.1 Site description
This study was conducted at the Old Woman Creek (OWC) National Estuarine Research Reserve (NERR) (https://ohiodnr.gov/wps/portal/gov/odnr/discover-and-learn/safety-conservation/about-ODNR/coastal-management/owc-nerr) in the western basin of Lake Erie. The Old Woman Creek estuary comprises fluvaquent and similar soils with silty textures set in Old Woman Creek's floodplain (Soil Survey Staff, 2021). The floodplain remains drowned because of the semi-permanent closure of the estuary mouth by a sand bar that controls occasional superficial exchanges of water and sediments between the Lake and estuary. However, year-to-decades long cycles of low and high-water levels are set by water levels of Lake Erie. The estuary margins are well-defined, and erosion of shorelines or other sediment sources from the surrounding upland area is not significant. A meteorological station at the site operated by NOAA NERR provides hourly long-term data, available through https://coast.noaa.gov/nerrs/reserves/old-woman-creek.html
An eddy covariance (EC) flux tower at the wetland provides half-hourly latent and sensible heat, water vapor, CO2 and CH4 fluxes and additional meteorological data, available through Ameriflux, site ID US-OWC https://ameriflux.lbl.gov/sites/siteinfo/US-OWC (Bohrer, 2016-), though EC flux data is not available for 2019, the core collection year. Additional CO2 and CH4 flux data from accumulation chambers, and dissolved CO2 and CH4 concentration profiles is available through ESS-DiVE (Bohrer et al., 2019).

2.2 Soil sampling and preparation
We focused on the northernmost section of the estuary to avoid the effects of the creek at the estuary mouth. We considered three transect locations with different sediment depositional conditions: “Outflow” near the outflow, “Backflow” at the outlet of the backwater flow, and “Middle” next to the main channel in the middle of the estuary. At each location, we set a transect with three relative microtopographic levels, corresponding to the categoric water depth at the core collection location: “Shallow”, “Intermediate”, and “Deep”. These levels were determined from a bathymetric survey conducted in 2019. In total, we had 9 coring locations, and at each location, we collected 4 cores of approximately 30 cm depth located at the corners of a 1x1 m square around the coring location. The cores were segmented to 1-cm (top 5 cm, for a finer resolution of the most recent years), or 2-cm (rest of core) increments. Each core segment was packed and shipped to the Ecohydrology and Forest-Meteorology Laboratory for further preparation and analysis. In the laboratory, samples were dried at 65 °C until constant weight and hand-grinded to powder with mortar and pestle. Distinguishable roots and other plant organs were removed during this process.

2.3 Soil dating and nutrient analyses
Core-depth chronologies for one core from each coring location were created from the distribution of 210Pb activity in the core profile and the constant-rate-of-supply (CRS) model (Appleby and Oldfield, 1978). The 210Pb activity of each segment of the dated core was determined using alpha-ray spectroscopy (Chronos Scientific Inc., CA) from 300 mg subsamples.
Total phosphorus concentrations were determined on dry, homogenized samples by hot acid digestion (1 mL sulfuric + 5 mL nitric acid, Hot Block, Environmental Express) followed by ICP-OES detection (Perkin Elmer).
Total carbon and nitrogen concentrations and 13C and 15 N isotopes for each depth increment were measured from one subsample (~3.5 mg) of each of the four cores in the stations. The subsamples were sent to the U. C. Davis Stable Isotope Facility where they were analyzed through dry combustion at 1080 °C, in a Micro Cube elemental analyzer with an infrared detector (Elementar Analysensysteme GmbH, Hanau, Germany) interfaced to either an Isoprime VisION IRMS (Elementar UK Ltd, Cheadle, UK) or a PDZ Europa 20-20 isotope ratio mass spectrometer (Sercon Ltd., Cheshire, UK).
